items.looks_like: Total loss of position data.
items.actually: Genuine coverage failure, tunnel or terrain shadowing, hardware fault, SIM or data plan failure, or regional interference not directed at this vehicle.
items.how_to_rule_out: Check whether other vehicles in the same area and time lost signal too. Broad regional loss indicates environmental or infrastructure causes; an isolated single-vehicle gap does not.

items.looks_like: Implausible position jumps.
items.actually: Known receiver artefacts, cold-start errors, multipath in urban canyons, or platform data-processing lag.
items.how_to_rule_out: Check whether the artefact appears across the fleet on the same hardware and firmware, which points to a technical rather than deliberate cause.

items.looks_like: Sustained regional GNSS interference.
items.actually: Documented wide-area interference affecting all users in a region, which is well reported in parts of Europe and is not aimed at any particular vehicle.
items.how_to_rule_out: Compare against published interference monitoring for the region and period before drawing any conclusion about a specific movement.

items.looks_like: An unattributable delivery signature.
items.actually: Genuine receipt by agency staff, a temporary worker, or a third-party site operator whom the consignee does not have on record.
items.how_to_rule_out: Ask the consignee who was actually on site in that window rather than only whether the name is on the authorised list.

items.looks_like: Handwritten annotations added to a consignment note.
items.actually: Legitimate reservations recorded at handover, which is exactly what the document is designed for.
items.how_to_rule_out: Establish when the annotation was made and by whom. Contemporaneous reservations are the correct use of the document; retrospective additions are not.

items.looks_like: The same reference appearing twice.
items.actually: A split delivery, a re-delivery after a failed attempt, or a documented partial movement.
items.how_to_rule_out: Check whether the duplication is explained by a recorded split or re-delivery event before treating it as reuse.

items.looks_like: A milestone or delivery stamp has no matching independent gate record.
items.actually: An asynchronous feed, a documented manual exception, a site-system outage or a legitimate handover outside the normal system path.
items.how_to_rule_out: Check the outage and exception logs, obtain the original CMR or consignee confirmation and record the reconciliation result before calling the stamp false.

items.looks_like: Contact details for an existing carrier have changed.
items.actually: Genuine rebranding, domain migration, office relocation, or acquisition.
items.how_to_rule_out: Confirm the change through the pre-existing channel, not the new one, and require confirmation from a known contact. A genuine change survives verification through the old channel; a takeover does not.

items.looks_like: Bank account name differs from the operator name.
items.actually: Legitimate use of a factoring company or a group treasury account, which is common in road freight.
items.how_to_rule_out: Require a written assignment or factoring agreement, and verify it with the factor directly. Legitimate factoring is documented and verifiable.

items.looks_like: A primary administrator or account owner changes shortly before a movement.
items.actually: A genuine ownership transfer, staff change, leave cover or managed-service transition.
items.how_to_rule_out: Verify the change through the previously known operator channel, record the effective date and preserve the old-to-new administrator audit trail.

items.looks_like: Total loss of position data.
items.actually: Genuine coverage failure, tunnel or terrain shadowing, hardware fault, SIM or data plan failure, or regional interference not directed at this vehicle.
items.how_to_rule_out: Check whether other vehicles in the same area and time lost signal too. Broad regional loss indicates environmental or infrastructure causes; an isolated single-vehicle gap does not.

items.looks_like: Implausible position jumps.
items.actually: Known receiver artefacts, cold-start errors, multipath in urban canyons, or platform data-processing lag.
items.how_to_rule_out: Check whether the artefact appears across the fleet on the same hardware and firmware, which points to a technical rather than deliberate cause.

items.looks_like: Sustained regional GNSS interference.
items.actually: Documented wide-area interference affecting all users in a region, which is well reported in parts of Europe and is not aimed at any particular vehicle.
items.how_to_rule_out: Compare against published interference monitoring for the region and period before drawing any conclusion about a specific movement.

items.looks_like: A tracker goes silent at a terminal or after a short stop.
items.actually: Battery failure, planned maintenance, coverage loss, wiring fault or a device replaced during a legitimate repair.
items.how_to_rule_out: Compare with fleet-wide outages, inspect the device and wiring, and reconcile the movement with independent records before attributing intent.

items.looks_like: Contact details for an existing carrier have changed.
items.actually: Genuine rebranding, domain migration, office relocation, or acquisition.
items.how_to_rule_out: Confirm the change through the pre-existing channel, not the new one, and require confirmation from a known contact. A genuine change survives verification through the old channel; a takeover does not.

items.looks_like: Bank account name differs from the operator name.
items.actually: Legitimate use of a factoring company or a group treasury account, which is common in road freight.
items.how_to_rule_out: Require a written assignment or factoring agreement, and verify it with the factor directly. Legitimate factoring is documented and verifiable.

items.looks_like: A primary administrator or account owner changes shortly before a movement.
items.actually: A genuine ownership transfer, staff change, leave cover or managed-service transition.
items.how_to_rule_out: Verify the change through the previously known operator channel, record the effective date and preserve the old-to-new administrator audit trail.

items.looks_like: A long unplanned stop in a high-risk area.
items.actually: A breakdown, traffic incident, border queue or enforced congestion stop, none of which the driver chose.
items.how_to_rule_out: Correlate with breakdown and incident reports and with traffic data for the corridor before treating a stop as a policy breach.

items.looks_like: Curtain damage at delivery.
items.actually: Accidental damage from loading equipment or road debris, which is common on soft-sided equipment.
items.how_to_rule_out: Compare the cut geometry and location with the load plan, and verify against seal and count records whether anything is actually missing.

items.looks_like: A loaded trailer is left at an unsecured location during a driver change or delay.
items.actually: A site closure, legally required rest, breakdown or documented relay where no loss occurred.
items.how_to_rule_out: Verify the instruction, coupling status, CCTV or receipt and the trailer condition at the next controlled handover before treating the stop as theft evidence.

items.looks_like: An unattributable delivery signature.
items.actually: Genuine receipt by agency staff, a temporary worker, or a third-party site operator whom the consignee does not have on record.
items.how_to_rule_out: Ask the consignee who was actually on site in that window rather than only whether the name is on the authorised list.

items.looks_like: Handwritten annotations added to a consignment note.
items.actually: Legitimate reservations recorded at handover, which is exactly what the document is designed for.
items.how_to_rule_out: Establish when the annotation was made and by whom. Contemporaneous reservations are the correct use of the document; retrospective additions are not.

items.looks_like: The same reference appearing twice.
items.actually: A split delivery, a re-delivery after a failed attempt, or a documented partial movement.
items.how_to_rule_out: Check whether the duplication is explained by a recorded split or re-delivery event before treating it as reuse.

items.looks_like: A milestone or delivery stamp has no matching independent gate record.
items.actually: An asynchronous feed, a documented manual exception, a site-system outage or a legitimate handover outside the normal system path.
items.how_to_rule_out: Check the outage and exception logs, obtain the original CMR or consignee confirmation and record the reconciliation result before calling the stamp false.

items.looks_like: Total loss of position data.
items.actually: Genuine coverage failure, tunnel or terrain shadowing, hardware fault, SIM or data plan failure, or regional interference not directed at this vehicle.
items.how_to_rule_out: Check whether other vehicles in the same area and time lost signal too. Broad regional loss indicates environmental or infrastructure causes; an isolated single-vehicle gap does not.

items.looks_like: Implausible position jumps.
items.actually: Known receiver artefacts, cold-start errors, multipath in urban canyons, or platform data-processing lag.
items.how_to_rule_out: Check whether the artefact appears across the fleet on the same hardware and firmware, which points to a technical rather than deliberate cause.

items.looks_like: Sustained regional GNSS interference.
items.actually: Documented wide-area interference affecting all users in a region, which is well reported in parts of Europe and is not aimed at any particular vehicle.
items.how_to_rule_out: Compare against published interference monitoring for the region and period before drawing any conclusion about a specific movement.

items.looks_like: A tracker goes silent at a terminal or after a short stop.
items.actually: Battery failure, planned maintenance, coverage loss, wiring fault or a device replaced during a legitimate repair.
items.how_to_rule_out: Compare with fleet-wide outages, inspect the device and wiring, and reconcile the movement with independent records before attributing intent.

items.looks_like: A newly registered company with no transport history bidding on freight.
items.actually: A genuine new entrant, or a newly incorporated vehicle of an existing operator restructuring its business.
items.how_to_rule_out: Verify operating authority directly with the issuing authority, confirm insurance with the insurer, and confirm that declared equipment exists and is registered to the entity. A real new entrant passes all three; a phantom fails at least one.

items.looks_like: A shared or serviced office address.
items.actually: Small legitimate hauliers and freight agents commonly use serviced offices while operating from a separate yard.
items.how_to_rule_out: Ask for the operational depot or parking location separately from the registered address, and verify that it exists and is capable of holding the declared fleet.

items.looks_like: An unattributable delivery signature.
items.actually: Genuine receipt by agency staff, a temporary worker, or a third-party site operator whom the consignee does not have on record.
items.how_to_rule_out: Ask the consignee who was actually on site in that window rather than only whether the name is on the authorised list.

items.looks_like: Handwritten annotations added to a consignment note.
items.actually: Legitimate reservations recorded at handover, which is exactly what the document is designed for.
items.how_to_rule_out: Establish when the annotation was made and by whom. Contemporaneous reservations are the correct use of the document; retrospective additions are not.

items.looks_like: The same reference appearing twice.
items.actually: A split delivery, a re-delivery after a failed attempt, or a documented partial movement.
items.how_to_rule_out: Check whether the duplication is explained by a recorded split or re-delivery event before treating it as reuse.

items.looks_like: A milestone or delivery stamp has no matching independent gate record.
items.actually: An asynchronous feed, a documented manual exception, a site-system outage or a legitimate handover outside the normal system path.
items.how_to_rule_out: Check the outage and exception logs, obtain the original CMR or consignee confirmation and record the reconciliation result before calling the stamp false.

items.looks_like: Sustained regional GNSS interference.
items.actually: Documented wide-area interference affecting all users in a region, which is well reported in parts of Europe and is not aimed at any particular vehicle.
items.how_to_rule_out: Compare against published interference monitoring for the region and period before drawing any conclusion about a specific movement.

items.looks_like: A tracker goes silent at a terminal or after a short stop.
items.actually: Battery failure, planned maintenance, coverage loss, wiring fault or a device replaced during a legitimate repair.
items.how_to_rule_out: Compare with fleet-wide outages, inspect the device and wiring, and reconcile the movement with independent records before attributing intent.

items.looks_like: Total loss of position data.
items.actually: Genuine coverage failure, tunnel or terrain shadowing, hardware fault, SIM or data plan failure, or regional interference not directed at this vehicle.

items.looks_like: Implausible position jumps.
items.actually: Known receiver artefacts, cold-start errors, multipath in urban canyons, or platform data-processing lag.
items.how_to_rule_out: Check whether the artefact appears across the fleet on the same hardware and firmware, which points to a technical rather than deliberate cause.

items.looks_like: Sustained regional GNSS interference.
items.actually: Documented wide-area interference affecting all users in a region, which is well reported in parts of Europe and is not aimed at any particular vehicle.
items.how_to_rule_out: Compare against published interference monitoring for the region and period before drawing any conclusion about a specific movement.

items.actually: Battery failure, planned maintenance, coverage loss, wiring fault or a device replaced during a legitimate repair.

items.looks_like: A newly registered company with no transport history bidding on freight.
items.actually: A genuine new entrant, or a newly incorporated vehicle of an existing operator restructuring its business.
items.how_to_rule_out: Verify operating authority directly with the issuing authority, confirm insurance with the insurer, and confirm that declared equipment exists and is registered to the entity. A real new entrant passes all three; a phantom fails at least one.

items.looks_like: A shared or serviced office address.
items.actually: Small legitimate hauliers and freight agents commonly use serviced offices while operating from a separate yard.
items.how_to_rule_out: Ask for the operational depot or parking location separately from the registered address, and verify that it exists and is capable of holding the declared fleet.

items.looks_like: Implausible position jumps.
items.actually: Known receiver artefacts, cold-start errors, multipath in urban canyons, or platform data-processing lag.
items.how_to_rule_out: Check whether the artefact appears across the fleet on the same hardware and firmware, which points to a technical rather than deliberate cause.

items.looks_like: Sustained regional GNSS interference.
items.actually: Documented wide-area interference affecting all users in a region, which is well reported in parts of Europe and is not aimed at any particular vehicle.
items.how_to_rule_out: Compare against published interference monitoring for the region and period before drawing any conclusion about a specific movement.

items.how_to_rule_out: Compare with fleet-wide outages, inspect the device and wiring, and reconcile the movement with independent records before attributing intent.

items.looks_like: A newly registered company with no transport history bidding on freight.
items.actually: A genuine new entrant, or a newly incorporated vehicle of an existing operator restructuring its business.
items.how_to_rule_out: Verify operating authority directly with the issuing authority, confirm insurance with the insurer, and confirm that declared equipment exists and is registered to the entity. A real new entrant passes all three; a phantom fails at least one.

items.looks_like: A shared or serviced office address.
items.actually: Small legitimate hauliers and freight agents commonly use serviced offices while operating from a separate yard.
items.how_to_rule_out: Ask for the operational depot or parking location separately from the registered address, and verify that it exists and is capable of holding the declared fleet.

items.looks_like: Total loss of position data.
items.actually: Genuine coverage failure, tunnel or terrain shadowing, hardware fault, SIM or data plan failure, or regional interference not directed at this vehicle.
items.how_to_rule_out: Check whether other vehicles in the same area and time lost signal too. Broad regional loss indicates environmental or infrastructure causes; an isolated single-vehicle gap does not.

items.looks_like: Implausible position jumps.
items.actually: Known receiver artefacts, cold-start errors, multipath in urban canyons, or platform data-processing lag.
items.how_to_rule_out: Check whether the artefact appears across the fleet on the same hardware and firmware, which points to a technical rather than deliberate cause.

items.looks_like: Sustained regional GNSS interference.
items.actually: Documented wide-area interference affecting all users in a region, which is well reported in parts of Europe and is not aimed at any particular vehicle.
items.how_to_rule_out: Compare against published interference monitoring for the region and period before drawing any conclusion about a specific movement.

items.looks_like: A tracker goes silent at a terminal or after a short stop.
items.actually: Battery failure, planned maintenance, coverage loss, wiring fault or a device replaced during a legitimate repair.
items.how_to_rule_out: Compare with fleet-wide outages, inspect the device and wiring, and reconcile the movement with independent records before attributing intent.

items.looks_like: Contact details for an existing carrier have changed.
items.actually: Genuine rebranding, domain migration, office relocation, or acquisition.
items.how_to_rule_out: Confirm the change through the pre-existing channel, not the new one, and require confirmation from a known contact. A genuine change survives verification through the old channel; a takeover does not.

items.looks_like: Bank account name differs from the operator name.
items.actually: Legitimate use of a factoring company or a group treasury account, which is common in road freight.
items.how_to_rule_out: Require a written assignment or factoring agreement, and verify it with the factor directly. Legitimate factoring is documented and verifiable.

items.looks_like: A primary administrator or account owner changes shortly before a movement.
items.actually: A genuine ownership transfer, staff change, leave cover or managed-service transition.
items.how_to_rule_out: Verify the change through the previously known operator channel, record the effective date and preserve the old-to-new administrator audit trail.

items.looks_like: An unattributable delivery signature.
items.actually: Genuine receipt by agency staff, a temporary worker, or a third-party site operator whom the consignee does not have on record.
items.how_to_rule_out: Ask the consignee who was actually on site in that window rather than only whether the name is on the authorised list.

items.looks_like: Handwritten annotations added to a consignment note.
items.actually: Legitimate reservations recorded at handover, which is exactly what the document is designed for.
items.how_to_rule_out: Establish when the annotation was made and by whom. Contemporaneous reservations are the correct use of the document; retrospective additions are not.

items.looks_like: The same reference appearing twice.
items.actually: A split delivery, a re-delivery after a failed attempt, or a documented partial movement.
items.how_to_rule_out: Check whether the duplication is explained by a recorded split or re-delivery event before treating it as reuse.

items.looks_like: A milestone or delivery stamp has no matching independent gate record.
items.actually: An asynchronous feed, a documented manual exception, a site-system outage or a legitimate handover outside the normal system path.
items.how_to_rule_out: Check the outage and exception logs, obtain the original CMR or consignee confirmation and record the reconciliation result before calling the stamp false.

items.looks_like: Total loss of position data.
items.actually: Genuine coverage failure, tunnel or terrain shadowing, hardware fault, SIM or data plan failure, or regional interference not directed at this vehicle.
items.how_to_rule_out: Check whether other vehicles in the same area and time lost signal too. Broad regional loss indicates environmental or infrastructure causes; an isolated single-vehicle gap does not.

items.looks_like: Implausible position jumps.
items.actually: Known receiver artefacts, cold-start errors, multipath in urban canyons, or platform data-processing lag.
items.how_to_rule_out: Check whether the artefact appears across the fleet on the same hardware and firmware, which points to a technical rather than deliberate cause.

items.looks_like: Sustained regional GNSS interference.
items.actually: Documented wide-area interference affecting all users in a region, which is well reported in parts of Europe and is not aimed at any particular vehicle.
items.how_to_rule_out: Compare against published interference monitoring for the region and period before drawing any conclusion about a specific movement.

items.looks_like: A tracker goes silent at a terminal or after a short stop.
items.actually: Battery failure, planned maintenance, coverage loss, wiring fault or a device replaced during a legitimate repair.
items.how_to_rule_out: Compare with fleet-wide outages, inspect the device and wiring, and reconcile the movement with independent records before attributing intent.

items.looks_like: Persistent shortages on a lane.
items.actually: A genuine count, labelling or system error at origin, or a units-of-measure mismatch between systems.
items.how_to_rule_out: Run a controlled count at origin and at destination for a defined period before treating the pattern as theft. Process error survives a controlled count; pilferage usually stops during it.

items.looks_like: Shortages concentrated on one driver.
items.actually: That driver is simply assigned disproportionately to the affected lane or shift.
items.how_to_rule_out: Normalise by exposure. Compare shortages per movement or per consignment handled, never absolute counts, and test whether the lane or the individual is the better explanation.

items.looks_like: Losses concentrated on high-value items.
items.actually: High-value items are more likely to be counted carefully and therefore more likely to have discrepancies detected at all.
items.how_to_rule_out: Compare detection rates as well as loss rates, and check whether low-value shortages are simply not being recorded.

items.how_to_rule_out: Verify operating authority directly with the issuing authority, confirm insurance with the insurer, and confirm that declared equipment exists and is registered to the entity. A real new entrant passes all three; a phantom fails at least one.

items.how_to_rule_out: Ask for the operational depot or parking location separately from the registered address, and verify that it exists and is capable of holding the declared fleet.

items.looks_like: Contact details for an existing carrier have changed.
items.actually: Genuine rebranding, domain migration, office relocation, or acquisition.
items.how_to_rule_out: Confirm the change through the pre-existing channel, not the new one, and require confirmation from a known contact. A genuine change survives verification through the old channel; a takeover does not.

items.looks_like: Bank account name differs from the operator name.
items.actually: Legitimate use of a factoring company or a group treasury account, which is common in road freight.
items.how_to_rule_out: Require a written assignment or factoring agreement, and verify it with the factor directly. Legitimate factoring is documented and verifiable.

items.looks_like: A primary administrator or account owner changes shortly before a movement.
items.actually: A genuine ownership transfer, staff change, leave cover or managed-service transition.
items.how_to_rule_out: Verify the change through the previously known operator channel, record the effective date and preserve the old-to-new administrator audit trail.

falsePositives.note: All 3 legitimate explanations the taxonomy documents for Carrier Identity Takeover, none withheld. They are not an exhaustive list of every innocent explanation, a ranking, and not a finding that this case is or is not one of them.

picks.text: Run automated lookalike-domain detection against the domains of onboarded carriers.
Notify the impersonated operator, which is a victim and will usually cooperate, and which may already hold evidence.

patternCountermeasures.note: Documented by the taxonomy against Carrier Identity Takeover, a pattern this case shares vocabulary with.
